curriculum.title: A Library That Tells One Story

core.big_idea: The Bible contains many books and genres that together tell God's connected story.

passages.reading_note: Read in its letter context as Paul addresses Timothy.
Notice Jesus' broad description of Israel's Scriptures and the gospel-shaped fulfilment.

core.metanarrative_position: Method: learning how the many biblical writings participate in one connected story centred on God's saving work in Christ.

claims.statement: Timothy had known the sacred writings from childhood, and those writings could make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
The passage describes Scripture as God-breathed and useful for teaching, correction, and training.
Jesus describes the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms as converging on His suffering, resurrection, and the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness.
The Bible is a library of different writings that together tell a connected story rather than a collection of unrelated moral tales.
These passages support confidence in Scripture but do not by themselves supply a complete list of the sixty-six books or eliminate the need to study canon history.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not claim that either passage directly prints the later table of contents.

core.interpretation_skill: Identify genre, speaker, audience, and the difference between a passage claim and a later synthesis.

learning.foundation_objective: Explain that the Bible contains many writings that together tell God's connected story and locate the two passages in their genres.
learning.extension_objective: Distinguish what 2 Timothy 3 and Luke 24 directly say from the broader inference that the whole canon functions as one library and story.
know: The Bible contains different kinds of writing.
Jesus connected Israel's Scriptures to His work and mission.
understand: Different genres require different reading habits.
A connected story does not mean every verse says exactly the same thing in the same way.
practise: Identify a Bible book's broad section before interpreting a passage.
Ask who is speaking, to whom, and why.
become: A student who approaches Scripture with confidence, care, and interpretive humility.
success_evidence: The student places at least six sample books into broad sections.
The student identifies the genres of 2 Timothy and Luke.
The student states one direct claim and one synthesis without confusing them.

zero_prep_card.objective: Students explain why the Bible is both a library and one connected story.
zero_prep_card.opening: Ask: How can a library contain many kinds of books but still have one subject area or purpose?
say: The Bible is not one modern book written at one time.
Its writings include narrative, law, poetry, prophecy, Gospels, letters, and apocalyptic literature.
Paul describes Scripture as God-breathed and useful; Jesus connects the Scriptures to His work and the mission that follows.
Reading responsibly means respecting each book's genre while tracing the connected story.
ask: What does Paul say Scripture does?
What broad sections does Jesus name?
What is the difference between a letter and a Gospel narrative?
Why can one-story reading still require context?
zero_prep_card.do: Complete the Bible Library Map with sample books and story anchors.
zero_prep_card.close: Pray for patience, humility, and growing understanding when reading Scripture.

preparation.passage_context: Second Timothy presents Paul's charge to Timothy amid false teaching and ministry pressure. Luke 24 narrates the risen Jesus explaining the Scriptures and commissioning witnesses. Neither passage is a generic publishing statement detached from its context.
text_observations: Second Timothy moves from Timothy's learned tradition and sacred writings to Scripture's usefulness and the equipped servant.
Luke 24 names Law, Prophets, and Psalms and connects fulfilment to suffering, resurrection, repentance, forgiveness, and mission.
The two passages have different genres and immediate purposes.
interpretation_notes: “Library” and “one story” are teaching syntheses, not phrases directly quoted from either text.
One-story reading must not erase the distinctive argument of each biblical book.
Canon history belongs later; this lesson should not overclaim what the passages settle.
theological_guardrails: Do not equate the teacher's interpretation with Scripture itself.
Do not teach that every narrative detail is a direct prediction of Jesus.
Do not present canon history as either irrelevant or simple.

likely_questions.question: Who decided which books are in the Bible?
likely_questions.purpose: Say this is an important historical question that later lessons will examine; do not improvise a simplistic answer.

likely_questions.question: Does every Old Testament story predict Jesus?
likely_questions.purpose: Explain that the whole story prepares for Christ, but not every detail is a prediction.

discussion_questions.question: What does 2 Timothy 3:14-17 directly say about Scripture?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Connect the uses to the letter's ministry setting.

discussion_questions.question: What sections and events appear in Luke 24:44-47?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: Name Law, Prophets, Psalms, suffering, and resurrection.

discussion_questions.question: What changes when we know whether a passage is poetry, narrative, or a letter?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Give one example of a genre-sensitive question.

discussion_questions.question: Which statement is direct text and which is synthesis: “Scripture is God-breathed” and “The Bible is one library telling one story”?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: Label the first direct and the second a synthesis.
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Explain why the synthesis may still be responsible.

activities.title: Bible Library Map
steps: Sort the sample books into broad sections.
Connect each sample book to one-story anchors.
Check one placement using a Bible table of contents.
Discuss what the map helps and what it cannot prove.
activities.learning_link: Builds canonical orientation and genre awareness.
activities.low_resource_alternative: Write section headings on the board and sort orally.

activities.title: Genre Question Match
steps: Match one reading question to each genre.
Explain why one question may not fit every genre.
activities.learning_link: Turns genre awareness into a reading habit.
activities.low_resource_alternative: Complete verbally with one example per genre.

closing.prayer_prompt: Ask for wisdom and humility in reading Scripture.
closing.take_home_line: Many writings, one connected story-read each part in context.

family.title: Many Books, One Story
family.parent_intro: This study introduces the Bible as a library whose writings participate in one connected story.

flow.instructions: Use the opening prompt to connect the lesson to ordinary family life.
Read 2 Timothy 3:14-17 and Luke 24:44-47. Identify which passage is a letter and which is a Gospel narrative.
Ask what each passage directly says before summarising the larger connection.
Place seven sample Bible books into broad sections using a table of contents.
Choose the weekly action, then pray together.

questions: What does Paul say Scripture is useful for?
Why should genre affect how we read?

interactive.title: Library Shelf
interactive.instructions: Sort Genesis, Psalms, Isaiah, Matthew, Acts, Romans, and Revelation into broad sections.

family.weekly_action: Before family Bible reading this week, name the book's genre and ask who is speaking to whom.
family.prayer: God, help us read Your word carefully, humbly, and faithfully.
family.parent_note: It is acceptable to say that canon history is a later question rather than forcing a quick answer.

quiz.question: What kind of writing is 2 Timothy?
quiz.explanation: Paul writes to Timothy in a ministry context.

quiz.question: Which broad sections does Jesus name in Luke 24?
quiz.explanation: Jesus uses a broad description of Israel's Scriptures.

quiz.question: True or false: every Bible book has the same genre.
Which statement is a broader synthesis?
options: The Bible is a library telling one connected story

answer.text: The Bible is a library telling one connected story

quiz.explanation: That sentence summarises multiple texts rather than quoting one verse.

puzzle.title: Book and Section
puzzle.instructions: Match each book with its broad section.

printables.title: Bible Library Map
printables.purpose: Canonical sections, genres, and metanarrative orientation

accessibility.plain_language_rule: Define genre as “a kind of writing” before using the technical term.
neurodiversity_supports: Keep the one-story arc visible throughout.
sensory_notes: No required performance or loud activity.
non_reader_support: Use book-name cards and coloured section labels.

do_not_ask: Do not require students to reveal private doubts or family disagreements about Scripture.
safeguarding.teacher_response: Welcome questions, distinguish what this lesson addresses from what it defers, and avoid shaming uncertainty.
